elements.label: Hotter, drier summers
elements.description: Summers with less rain and more evaporation. Around 2050 (2036–2065), against 1991–2020, every KNMI'23 scenario has 2 to 13% less summer rain, 6 to 11% more potential evaporation in summer and a largest precipitation deficit of April to September 13 to 35% larger (KNMI, 2023, p. 4), and lower summer discharges of the great rivers are among the risks for this century it gives from the earlier risk assessment (p. 42). Measured as national averages, evaporation over five stations, Vlissingen among them (p. 5): this report gives no rain or deficit number for Zeeland, which appears only on maps of the whole country, West Europe or Europe, in colour classes, for the present and around 2100 (pp. 15, 24, 27). Set outside the island: a Constant.
elements.simplification: Counts the summer's dryness on the island and in the great rivers as one driver: the summer rain and evaporation that the rainwater lens and the crops' water need follow, and the rivers' summer discharge that Fresh water supplied to the island depends on. Around 2050 summer rain falls and evaporation rises in every KNMI'23 scenario (KNMI, 2023, p. 4), and lower summer discharges of the great rivers are among the risks for this century it gives from the earlier risk assessment (p. 42), so each link out keeps its sign; a summer dry on the island with the rivers still full, or the reverse, cannot be drawn. A Constant has no link in, so no loop runs through it.

elements.label: Sea-level rise
elements.description: The mean level of the sea at the Dutch coast. Around 2050 (2036–2065) every KNMI'23 scenario has it 16 to 38 cm above 1995–2014, 24 cm in the low-emission scenarios and 27 cm in the high, still rising by 1 to 8 mm a year (KNMI, 2023, pp. 3, 5). Set outside the island: a Constant.

elements.label: Wetter winters
elements.description: More rain in winter. Around 2050 (2036–2065), against 1991–2020, every KNMI'23 scenario has 4 to 7% more winter rain, and 0.4 to 0.8 more days a winter with 10 mm or more (KNMI, 2023, p. 3). Measured as a national average over 13 rain stations (p. 5): this report gives no number for Zeeland, which appears only on maps of Europe and West Europe around 2100, in colour classes (pp. 15, 24). Set outside the island: a Constant.

elements.label: Rainwater lens thickness in the low polders
elements.description: The thickness of the fresh rainwater lenses on top of the saline groundwater in the island's low polders, from the surface to the middle of the mixing zone between them: about 2 m on average in the low-lying polders with saline seepage, under 2 m over more than half of the 56 km² surveyed (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3667, 3672–3673, 3675, measured on the island from a helicopter and on the ground). These lenses keep salt out of the root zone and reach only the crop on their own field. A Stock: a year's recharge barely moves it (the links into it from Hotter, drier summers, Wetter winters, Soil structure and Winter rain drained away).

elements.label: Polder surface elevation (NAP)
elements.description: The land surface elevation of the island's polders relative to NAP, lowered by subsidence: most of the low polders' surface lies around NAP (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10), the western low polders mostly between −1 and −2 m NAP and the eastern ones at about 0 to +1 m (pp. 27–28), the middle and east of Schouwen between −1.5 and −0.5 m NAP (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 22), and Zeeland's lowest polders at −1.5 to −2.5 m relative to mean sea level (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3661, for the province). Tidal silt, let in through a wisselpolder, would barely raise it on this island: the Grevelingen has no tide, and the Oosterschelde has too little silt to raise polders on a large scale (De Mesel et al., 2013). Since the storm surge barrier its channels carry 52–70% less suspended sediment (Ma et al., 2014, p. 15); near Zierikzee the water holds under 10 mg/l, presumably mostly fine sand, and on the Oosterschelde's salt marshes 3–10 mm settles a year, about −1 to 5 mm after compaction (van Maldegem & de Jong, 2004, pp. 14, 27–28), against 16–32 mm a year on young marshes along the Westerschelde in 1931–1955 and 4–18 mm in 1955–2002 (De Mesel et al., 2013, p. 25).

elements.label: Root zone salinity
elements.description: The salt concentration of the soil water in the crop root zone. Salt harms a crop in two phases: at once osmotically, slowing the growth of young leaves, and more slowly as sodium (Na+) or chloride (Cl-) builds up in the leaves, ageing the older ones early (Munns & Tester, 2008, pp. 654–656, a review of plant physiology, which holds wherever the crop grows). It rises in a dry summer as the soil dries out and salt rises by capillary rise, and falls with the winter's rain surplus, which in one winter washes the topsoil of most well-drained soils free enough of salt to be cropped, and that of badly drained soil in two, exceptionally three (van Beekom et al., 1953a, pp. 155–158, measured after the floods in Zeeland): within the year where the soil drains well, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Saline seepage (kwel)
elements.description: The upward flow of salt groundwater from the sand below into the clay and peat top layer of the island's polders, in mm a day, which leaves through drains, ditches and evaporation (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3662). The higher water pressure at depth drives it in the low polders, where it keeps the rainwater lenses thin, mostly under 2 m, and the shallow groundwater brackish to salt (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10); below the lens its water holds 10 to 16 g of chloride a litre (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675), against about 16 to 17 g in North Sea water (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Most of Duiveland gets salt seepage, most in its low parts near the Oosterschelde (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 27); in the western low polders it is strongest near the Grevelingen and the Oosterschelde (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). The flow follows the water pressures, which change constantly with recharge and drainage (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3675): within the year, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Soil structure
elements.description: The soil's aggregates and pores, which set how fast water soaks in: well-drained clay with its structure intact let the winter's rain surplus soak through almost completely, while clay whose structure sodium had broken down became impervious and sticky when wet (van Beekom et al., 1953a, p. 157; 1953b, pp. 230, 233, measured after the floods in Zeeland). A Stock: once broken down, it recovers over years (Root zone salinity → Soil structure). Workability, which structure and wetness both shape, is Spring workability of the fields.
elements.simplification: Draws the salt as the only driver of Soil structure. It leaves out the smearing and compaction of soil worked too wet, which Spring workability of the fields describes, because that damage comes from when and how the soil is worked, not from the salt or the fresh water, and no source on this element shows how much it adds on the island. Leaving it out removes an inflow and folds no step: every drawn link keeps its sign, and R1 stays reinforcing. A feedback from poor workability back to structure, if farmers work the soil while it is still wet, is not drawn.

elements.label: Upconing of salt groundwater
elements.description: The rise of salt groundwater towards a well that pumps fresh water from a lens floating on it, in a cone under the well. In Zeeland fresh groundwater is mostly pumped through horizontal wells (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 1), and the water board's general rule caps a farm's pumping at 800 m³ per hectare a year, to keep the fresh stock and stop the fresh-salt boundary rising (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9 and its explanation). In the Freshmaker pilot on a creek ridge at Ovezande, Zuid-Beveland, the pumped water grew saltier during each pumping season, which the report explains by the lens thinning and the cone possibly reaching the shallow well (Oude Essink et al., 2018, p. 67); in a model of the creek ridge at Serooskerke, Walcheren, the cone had not settled after ten years (p. 58), the slow part being the lens itself (Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges, a Stock). The island's creek ridges hold the same kind of lens, rain soaked in over salt groundwater (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). Deltares, modelling Zeeland's rules in 2018, found that on the whole they seem enough to prevent strong salinisation under and around a well (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021, answer 3). Within the season: an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Farmers' demand for deep polder drainage
elements.description: Farmers' wish for low ditch levels, so that their fields drain: dry enough for heavy machinery to work them, which holding water back for dry times sometimes makes hard (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021c, p. 44), and free of water damage after heavy rain, which farmers in the island's western low polders often find a bigger problem than drought (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27). They put it to the water board as it prepares its water level plans, which it does with interest groups such as farming, and in views on a draft (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 17): on Duiveland's draft of 2021, four views feared that a raise the plan proposed to study would bring more flooding in extreme rain (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 53). Heavier summer downpours have no variable of their own and enter here: around 2050 the hour of summer rain exceeded once a year, 16 mm now, is 4 to 11% heavier in the four KNMI'23 scenarios (ranges 2 to 16%), with fewer light showers and more heavy ones, measured nationally (KNMI, 2023, pp. 4, 26), and many of the island's farmers still rate the risk of waterlogging above that of drought, since it can make or break a harvest in a short time (Raat et al., 2026, p. 23). Within the year, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Fresh water supplied to the island
elements.description: Fresh water brought to the island's farms from outside it in the growing season (present in Tholen and Zeeuws-Vlaanderen; absent on Walcheren, the Bevelanden and Schouwen-Duiveland). It needs a supply route, and in drought it is what the national distribution leaves for the route to carry. Rijkswaterstaat makes that distribution: in drought it divides the little fresh water of the large rivers and lakes among the users through weirs, pumping stations and sluices, by the verdringingsreeks when there is too little for all, and the greater part of Zeeland lies outside the area it can supply (Rijkswaterstaat, n.d.).

elements.label: Freshwater availability for crops
elements.description: Fresh water crops can draw on in the growing season: rain, the soil moisture and groundwater of the field above the lens, water farmers pump or have stored, and water supplied from outside, which reaches the island nowhere now (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 4, 8). A Stock: water held in the root zone and in storage carries over from day to day: the root zone's is a daily balance, what the day before left plus rain, irrigation and capillary rise, less what the crop uses and what drains below the roots (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8, eq. 85). It fills and empties within the season.

elements.label: Freshwater storage measures
elements.description: The fresh water a year that the measures in place on the island's farms keep, store or collect for the growing season. They work three ways (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 16–23, 53, for the island): in the low polders, controlled drainage and anti-salinisation drainage (Drains2Buffer) keep the thin rainwater lens against salt, their water staying in the field's own soil, where it cannot be pumped (pp. 33, 53), and weirs in ditches keep the lens in flat areas drained by ditches with a moderate to large drooglegging (pp. 16, 19); on the creek ridges, the dunes and where a sand layer lies under the clay, the creek-ridge infiltration system, the Freshmaker and underground storage under a clay layer infiltrate winter water to pump in summer (pp. 20–22, 38); and double drainage, a concept the study shows only in model simulations, not yet tested in practice, would collect fresh drain water into a basin to irrigate from (pp. 23, 29, 32). An adaptive practice: measures to keep more fresh water in the ground as drought and salinisation increase (p. 4). The study set out from their being not yet fitted to the island and too risky for many farms to invest in alone (pp. 4, 11), and concluded that more is possible than the farmers first thought (pp. 5, 55). A Stock: a measure, once built, lasts 15 to 30 years (pp. 17–22, 34). The farm decides a measure; infiltrating water needs the water board's permit (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, art. 4.5 lid 2), a weir the neighbours' consent, and raising a ditch's level the water board's cooperation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 26, 44–45). Whether a farm wants to store weighs storing against its other ways through a dry summer (pumping, other crops), where capacity to invest is whether it can. Stored water pays back over years, which suits a farm that owns its land more than one on a short lease; and where stored water spreads under the neighbours, one farm pays and others gain. Whether either holds a farm back is a question for the group model building session. No measure is enough alone: on the island the current freshwater measures and innovations supply too little, are no one-size-fits-all solution, fit only a limited part of it, have not yet proven their value and are costly (Delphy, 2023, p. 50), each is custom work, and not every farmer takes them up (p. 40). Beside the farms, Acacia Water, Deltares and Delphy shape it: in a demonstration with the trial farm Rusthoeve and the municipality, double drainage was laid on two test plots at Kerkwerve and anti-salinisation drainage on one at Dreischor, on three of the island's farms (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, 2023), the EU's rural development programme paying half of the cost and the knowledge parties a part of it (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-b). Measures of these kinds are among the drought adaptation measures van Duinen et al. (2015a, p. 1085) list for farmers in the south-west Netherlands, from a survey of 2013: drains set deeper or regulated, a deep drain for salt, a storage basin, extraction from creek ridges and injection into a deep aquifer.
elements.simplification: Counts the measures of three kinds as one quantity, the fresh water a year they keep, store or collect, each kind reaching crops by its own link out: to Winter rain drained away, to Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges and dunes, and to Freshwater availability for crops. It assumes every kind responds alike to the drivers into this element. Every loop through it keeps its polarity and its mechanism; what it leaves out is that a rise in one kind need not be a rise in another, so the semi-quantitative analysis cannot vary them apart.

elements.label: Groundwater extraction for irrigation
elements.description: Fresh water farmers pump from the fresh groundwater through their own wells, to irrigate in summer; the water board's pumping stations belong to drainage. How much and from where is Pumping the water board allows. Whose lens a well draws on, the farm's own or one it shares with its neighbours, so that a farm pumping less leaves water to them, is a hypothesis for the group model building session; the rules are written so that a well's effects stay within the farm's own field (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021), an aim of the rules rather than a measurement. Irrigation and a well into a phreatic aquifer are among the drought adaptation measures van Duinen et al. (2015a, p. 1085) list for farmers in the south-west Netherlands, from a survey of 2013. Pumping follows the season's shortfall within the year: an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Objections to land-use plans
elements.description: The views and appeals against the plans for the island's water and land while a plan is pending, the water board's level plans among them, which can slow, change or stop it. On a level plan, the views come in the six weeks its draft lies open and are answered in the decision, and anyone affected may appeal at the court for six weeks after it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 17–18). No source read gives the routes for the other bodies' plans.

elements.label: Winter rain drained away
elements.description: Rain in winter that field drains carry off in the island's low polders instead of refilling their rainwater lens: tile drains usually discharge shallow groundwater rapidly during rain, as other studies found (de Louw et al., 2011, p. 3661), and on Schouwen-Duiveland a large part of the year's rain is drained away in the wet season (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 54), a figure for the whole island, of which this counts the low polders' share. What the drains carry off the creek ridges and dunes acts on their own lens instead (Polder drainage depth → Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges and dunes). It follows each rain, within the year: an Auxiliary.
elements.simplification: Counts as drained away the winter rain the drains carry off the farm toward the ditches and the pumping stations, and reads every drop less of it as rain that refills the rainwater lens. That holds for the measures that keep water in the field's soil, but not for double drainage, whose shallow drains collect fresh drain water into a basin (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 23): that water neither leaves the farm nor refills the lens, so the link from Freshwater storage measures overstates what refills the lens for that share, while the water itself reaches crops by Freshwater storage measures' own link to Freshwater availability for crops. B6 and R4 keep their polarity, since a measure that catches water raises the water crops get either way, and their mechanism, which runs through the measures that keep rain in the field.

elements.label: Crop yield
elements.description: The yield per hectare of the conventional crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) that sells, the kilograms in the sizes and grades buyers pay for, under the prevailing freshwater, soil and workability conditions; what salt takes from their harvest is Harvest lost to salt. The island's arable farms grow potatoes, onions, sugar beet, cereals, grass seed and vegetables in rotation (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 30, 38, from the farms studied), and some in the low polders have stopped growing sown onions for the salt (p. 31). A season's harvest: an Auxiliary.
elements.simplification: The current crops (potatoes, onions, sugar beet) are one yield per hectare. Each yields less with a larger water shortfall, worse soil structure or fields that cannot be worked in time, so every link into the yield keeps its sign for each crop and no loop through it changes. What one yield leaves out: the crops lose in different proportions (the yield response factors on Crop water shortfall → Crop yield), and farms can shift their rotation among them, as some in the low polders stopped growing sown onions for the salt.

elements.label: Market demand for alternative crops
elements.description: Consumer demand for new or alternative crops (e.g. protein crops); the contracts buyers offer for them are drawn apart (Buyer contracts for new crops). For quinoa the market is small: in Flanders it is sold under contract at €1,100 a tonne on a local market still very limited, with no forecast yet of how demand for local quinoa will grow (Cloet et al., 2024, pp. 2–3); in the Netherlands a supermarket has its own-brand quinoa from 12 Dutch farmers under a three-year contract, Dutch quinoa costing more to buy in than imported (DutchNews.nl, 2026). For protein crops, Rabobank expects demand for plant-based meat and dairy alternatives to grow towards 2030, while yields lower than in other countries and a quality that often misses food standards, which keeps the price low, limit what they earn (Polman et al., 2026, p. 8). For halophytes such as samphire and sea aster, grown in a few places in Zeeland, the food market is small and easily saturated, and offers farmers no lasting market potential (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6). Measured in Flanders, the Netherlands and Zeeland, none on the island. Whether demand, rather than local processing capacity, is what holds the new crops back on the island is open: no source read weighs the two. A Constant: the island's farmers cannot move it.

elements.label: Local processing capacity for new crops
elements.description: Plants and supply chains in Zeeland, on the island or near it, that store, process or sell new crops. Breeding of tolerant varieties is Yield of salt-tolerant varieties on offer. No source read shows a new crop processed on the island. Sea vegetables are sorted and packed, mostly by hand, by a grower and trader at Nieuw- en Sint Joosland, who in 2018 shipped most of his sea fennel, seaweed and sea spaghetti to organic shops and was investing, with a colleague from Schouwen-Duiveland, in growing new sea greens in greenhouses to supply international restaurants and supermarkets directly (FreshPlaza, 2018); at Colijnsplaat an arable farmer and a trader of sea vegetables founded a company, NZZT, to grow sea crops and set up their supply chain, in a project of 2020–2021 (EU CAP Network, 2023). GreenFood50 runs its quinoa chain, from grower to customer, from Wageningen, and has its quinoa grown close to its processing facilities (GreenFood50, n.d.), and a Zeeland quinoa chain was a project from 2021 to 2024 (De Vriend, 2024a). Buyers and processors build or keep it where they find it worthwhile against processing the crops elsewhere.
elements.simplification: Counts the chains of every new crop as one capacity, though each is built for one kind of crop, sea vegetables (FreshPlaza, 2018) or quinoa (GreenFood50, n.d.): it leaves out that a crop's harvest makes only a chain for its own kind worthwhile and that a chain cuts the haul only for the crops it takes. Per kind of crop the loop R7 runs through the same positive links, so it stays reinforcing with the same mechanism; the total makes R7 look easier to start where farms spread their hectares over crops that no single chain takes. It also draws the capacity as answering only to the harvest within reach and market demand, and leaves out public support for setting up a chain, such as the LEADER climate adaptation support for the project in which NZZT at Colijnsplaat set up its chain for sea crops (EU CAP Network, 2023). Such support would enter as one more positive driver beside the link from the harvest and closes no loop, so R7 keeps its sign and its mechanism. It splits the plants and chains that take new crops by distance into this variable, those in Zeeland, and Processing of new crops elsewhere, those outside it, and leaves out that the haul, and with it the net price, still changes with distance within each side. More capacity on the near side still cuts the haul, so R7 keeps its sign and its mechanism.

elements.label: Fields moved to new crops
elements.description: Hectares the island's farmers move from their current crops to new crops, which cope with salt or with little fresh water, in a year. The farmers decide it field by field: they move a field where they find a new crop worthwhile against their current crops; capacity to invest is whether they can, and dependence on the current crops what holds them. Switching to salt- or drought-resistant crop types is among the drought adaptation measures van Duinen et al. (2015a, p. 1085) list for farmers in the south-west Netherlands, from a survey of 2013. What a switch costs falls in the year a field moves (Fields moved to new crops → Farmers' capacity to invest); the field then stays under its new crop in Adoption of new crops. Not every new crop eases the water limit: the crops often suggested as possibly less sensitive to drought, fibre crops and legumes such as hemp, flax and field beans, earn about what winter wheat does or less, sown in spring they carry more risk, and flax needs water too, so the crops for a biobased economy will probably shift the crop plans a little but solve no water problem (Delphy, 2023, p. 48); quinoa copes with little water (Adoption of new crops). An Auxiliary: a year's flow into that Stock.

elements.label: Adoption of new crops
elements.description: Hectares under crops new to the island's rotations that cope with salt or with little fresh water. On the parcels studied in the island's low polders the rotations hold potato, onion, sugar beet, cereals and grass seed (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 30), and no source read shows a new crop grown on the island. Elsewhere in Zeeland, most still experimental and small (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 57): samphire and sea aster, irrigated with saline water on the edges of salt marshes at Emmadorp, Waterdunen and Wolphaarsdijk, labour intensive and seasonal, their sales low (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6); sea fennel and sea banana on an arable farm at Colijnsplaat, where a new company worked out how to grow them, in fields and greenhouses, and set up their supply chain (EU CAP Network, 2023). Quinoa copes with both: it grows to maturity on irrigation water of more than 250 mM NaCl (van Loo, 2023, p. 77), has a moderate need for water and still yields 2,000 kg of grain a hectare on 270 mm of available water (p. 75, from Çolak et al., 2021), and keeps drawing water from the soil under long drought (p. 77); it is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine, but needs a fine seed bed, and its row distance, 15 to 50 cm, depends on how the farmer controls weeds (p. 75). Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against their current crops; capacity to invest is whether they can, and dependence on the current crops what holds them. Switching to salt- or drought-resistant crop types is among the drought adaptation measures van Duinen et al. (2015a, p. 1085) list for farmers in the south-west Netherlands, from a survey of 2013. A Stock: a field keeps its crop through the season, and farmers move fields to a new crop over years (Fields moved to new crops), as they come to see the damage over dry summers (Harvest lost to salt → Fields moved to new crops) and, a hypothesis, as their crops fall short of water (Crop water shortfall → Fields moved to new crops).
elements.simplification: Counts the hectares of every new crop in the island's rotations as one area, those that cope with salt and those that cope with little fresh water, and lets them act alike on each link out, while the crops differ: quinoa is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine (van Loo, 2023, p. 75), sea fennel and sea banana were grown in a pilot at Colijnsplaat, in test fields and greenhouses, with a food supply chain set up for them (EU CAP Network, 2023, pp. 1–2), and samphire and sea aster are labour intensive, their sales low (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6). It abstracts in summing the hectares and idealizes in R7, where one crop's harvest draws a chain that raises every new crop's net price, while a chain for one crop raises only that crop's price. Salt losses move fields to a crop that copes with salt (B2), a shortfall of water, a hypothesis, to one that copes with little water, and a crop that copes with both, as quinoa does (van Loo, 2023, pp. 75, 77), answers both. No crop reverses a sign, so B2, R6, B10 and R7 keep their polarity and their mechanism, each running crop by crop; what it leaves out is how hard each crop pulls in each loop.

elements.label: Agricultural land value
elements.description: The price unlet farmland on the island sells for (€/ha), set by what buyers expect to earn from it. A buyer bids at most what an extra hectare can earn back over the years of the investment (Farjon et al., 2013, box Maximale biedprijs), and the price is set for an important part by what expanding farms earn on extra hectares, their income and expectations combined with what they can borrow: scale enlargement and low interest rates hold it up, swings in what the land earns and limits on banks' financing of land press it down (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, pp. 1–3). So the price of farmland in the Netherlands has risen far faster than what the land earns on average: the nominal price more than tenfold since 1970, net value added two to three times (Farjon et al., 2013, introduction). Farmers bought 54% of the land traded in the Netherlands from 2012 to early 2023 and investors 9%, whose purchases, as a share of the farmland, are highest in Noord-Holland, Zuid-Holland and Zeeland; in Zeeland on average just over 1.5% of the farmland is sold on the free market in a year (Kuiper et al., 2023, pp. 1–2, Appendix 1). Banks hold it as security for their loans (Farjon et al., 2013, section Financiering van bedrijfsuitbreiding). No source read gives the island's land prices.
elements.simplification: A soil's structure enters the land's value only through what the land earns (Soil structure → Crop yield → Farm income → this element), the sign the same, since buyers price what they expect it to earn. What it leaves out: any value a buyer gives good soil beyond its income.

elements.label: Risk premium on farm loans
elements.description: The part of a farm loan's interest that differs between clients: the specific premium a bank charges above the base rate, which banks also call the credit or risk premium. The loan's risk sets it for a large part: the interest holds, per client, the bank's expected losses on the loan and the cost of the capital the banks' solvency rules require it to hold against it, both higher the higher the credit risk the bank sees; on a loan with a fixed rate it may be part of one total rate (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a, n.d.-b). The capital those rules require is set by the EU: its banking package puts the final Basel III standards into EU law, the new rules of the Capital Requirements Regulation applying from 1 January 2025 (European Commission, Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union, 2023), and by the EBA's estimate EU banks' minimum Tier 1 capital requirement is 9.0% higher at full implementation in 2028 (European Banking Authority, 2023); no source read shows climate or salinisation risk in the risk weights of farm loans. No source read gives the premiums banks charge the island's farms.
elements.simplification: Folds Basel IV capital requirements, a Constant on no loop with one link, into this description: the capital rules are context for the premium, set by the EU outside the CLD's scale, and no actor in the CLD can move them. No loop runs through it, no actor inside the scale loses a decision and no delay is lost; what it leaves out is a change in the rules as a driver the semi-quantitative analysis could vary.

elements.label: Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops
elements.description: The share of the rotation under the high-value cash crops salt harms most, seed and ware potatoes and sown onions (Root zone salinity → Harvest lost to salt). Potatoes are financially attractive and sensitive to the climate, the most important crop of Dutch arable farming (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 12): on specialised arable farms on clay growing ware potatoes they bring in, on average over the years, 55% of the arable revenue, ware potatoes 32% and seed potatoes 23%, against 14% for onions and 11% for sugar beet (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 14). In Zeeland, a manager of the cooperative CZAV says, a farmer earns his money not with rotation crops but with onions, beets and potatoes (Economic Board Zeeland, 2023, p. 19). The guideline is potatoes on a field at most one year in three, against potato cyst nematode (one in two for starch potatoes), so a farm growing more of them rents or swaps land (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 4). On the parcels studied in the island's low polders, where the seepage pressure is high and the surface water salty all year, the rotations hold potato, onion, sugar beet, cereals and grass seed, the farmers have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions, and with more fresh water they would be open to more profitable crops (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 30–31). In Zeeland the sown onions halved from 4,705 ha in 2019 to 2,579 in 2024 after dry summers, poor harvests and a lack of fresh water, which four in five arable farmers have no access to, while potatoes held at about 19,000 ha (De Vriend, 2024b). A Stock: the share holds through the season and shifts over years (Root zone salinity → Dependence on high-margin salt-sensitive crops).

elements.label: Farm income
elements.description: Farms' income from their crops: the revenue from crop sales, set by yield and prices, minus the costs they pay (rent, interest, the water board's levy, their own pumping) and depreciation, as Dutch farm accounts measure it (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 21), per hectare in a year. Dutch arable farms earned about 65,000 euro per unpaid labour unit on average over 2010–2016, spread widely: in 2016 a fifth had a negative income and as many earned more than 100,000 euro (pp. 21–22). In 2025 an estimated 60,000 euro, lower prices after good harvests in north-west Europe and beyond outweighing the yields (van der Meulen, 2025). No source read gives the island's farm incomes.

elements.label: Farmers' capacity to invest
elements.description: What a farm can put into an investment: its savings, built up from what is left of its income after the household's spending and its payment obligations, repayments included, and the credit a bank will give it. A farm whose income is negative cannot reserve enough for investment (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 25), and one short of cash first cuts maintenance and private spending or draws on its savings, and if that is not enough can ask its bank to defer part of its interest and repayments or for more credit (p. 28); banks judge more and more whether a farm's operations earn enough to meet all its financial obligations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). Machines, implements and installations are the main category of Dutch arable farms' investment (p. 19), and irrigation systems cost relatively much to install, not always within a farmer's reach (Verhagen et al., 2018, p. 28).

elements.label: Financial leverage
elements.description: The farm's debt relative to the value of its assets, the inverse of its solvency (equity as a share of total capital). Land is 70% of an arable farm's balance sheet (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 13), so the ratio moves with the land price: arable farms' solvency was 81% in 2018 because their land had risen in value, while their long-term debt had tripled since 2001 to 770,000 euro per farm, and it differs widely between farms (p. 21). Farms that expanded recently have a lower solvency, and large arable farms, of about 190 ha on average in 2015, about 70% against 80% for arable farming as a whole in 2010–2015 (Silvis & Voskuilen, 2017, p. 3); farms that own little of their land gain little from a rising land price but owe much less (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 26).

elements.label: Arable land in the polders
elements.description: Hectares of the island's land under arable crops, the census's akkerbouw, conventional or salt-tolerant and fallow included, whoever owns it: 9,094 ha in 2025 against 11,395 ha in 2000, on farms whose main seat is on the island (CBS, 2026). The farms growing them halved over those years, from 402 to 200, so the hectares per farm rose from 28 to 45: land from a farm that stops mostly goes in parts to neighbouring farms that are expanding, which can pay the most for it (Luijt, 2007, p. 25, nationally). The fall in hectares is net, the census's farmland 906 ha smaller and its grass and forage crops 1,431 ha larger (CBS, 2026). It falls when the land's holder, present or next, stops growing arable crops on it; what the land becomes then (nature, grassland, water storage) waits for the group's system boundary.

elements.label: Crop water shortfall
elements.description: What crops need in the growing season beyond the water they get: the gap farmers' water decisions respond to. What a crop needs, whatever the water's origin, is the water it uses when it has enough, its evapotranspiration, set by the weather (radiation, air temperature, humidity and wind speed) and by the crop and its stage of growth (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56, a guide to crop water use that holds wherever the crop grows). The island's farms depend wholly on rain and on the fresh groundwater under the dunes, the creek ridges and the thin rainwater lenses of the low polders; with no link to the main freshwater system, no fresh water can be brought in and no ditches flushed in dry periods, so the farms run short of water, as the dry years 2018, 2019 and 2020 showed (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8). It follows the weather within the season: an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland's call for a supply route
elements.description: How firmly Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland, ZLTO's branch on the island, asks the province, the municipality and the water board for a route bringing fresh water to the island. After a report on the island's freshwater demand, which it commissioned and paid for (Delphy, 2023, p. 1), it called a pipeline from the Haringvliet the one solution (Omroep Zeeland, 2023), and its chair, an arable farmer, looks for more fresh water with the municipality and the province (van Essen, 2026). An Auxiliary: it follows the shortfall farmers report and holds nothing of its own.

elements.label: Freshwater supply route to the island
elements.description: Pipes or channels that could bring fresh water to the island, as their capacity in a summer; none exists. Provincie Zeeland, the actor here as the only body shown acting on the island's route, had a pipeline explored after the farming sector pressed for one (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, p. 7); the study leaves open who pays and who would run it (p. 51), and no source read shows a decision. Once one is decided on, the study expects implementing the main supply pipeline to take about 3 to 10 years depending on the variant, and the distribution on the island within 2 to 3 years by a ring pipeline or about 5 to 10 years through watercourses that need widening, naming the time needed for permits, land acquisition and further engineering among what lengthens it (Witteveen+Bos, 2021, pp. 43–44, 46–47). By law a project decision can come from the water board's executive, for its water tasks, the province's or a minister (Omgevingswet, 2026, art. 5.44), and the water board may charge the farmland a supply project serves up to 100% more, once at least half of its owners have responded and two thirds of those are in favour (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 122); it charges more for its supply projects on Tholen and Sint Philipsland and in the Reigersbergsche polder (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026c, arts. 5–6). IenW shapes it twice: its minister allots the Delta Fund, from which a freshwater region can claim 25% of a regional measure's cost, in principle up to 50% for an innovative one or one carried out by several regions (Algemene Rekenkamer, 2026, p. 32), a contribution the minister and state secretary decided in October 2026 to stop: the Delta Programme Freshwater goes on at 50% of its initial reservation, EUR 284 million less, aimed at the main water system, its contributions and subsidies for the regional water system stopped and its current phase completed as planned, the money freed going to the letter's tasks, above all maintaining and renewing the infrastructure built after the Second World War, and the budget processed partly at the Voorjaarsnota 2027 (Minister van Infrastructuur en Waterstaat & Staatssecretaris van Infrastructuur en Waterstaat, 2026, Table 9, the opening and section Tot slot); and the Delta Programme 2027, under the Delta Commissioner's direction and presented by the minister with the Delta Fund's budget, proposes that the south-west delta's areas with no supply from outside speed up their way to self-sufficiency, the region open to exploring small extensions of the supplied area that add evident value, are future-proof and keep the extra demand on the Volkerak-Zoommeer limited, the demand on the Hollandsch Diep and Haringvliet not raised (Ministerie van Infrastructuur en Waterstaat et al., 2026, pp. 4, 88–89).

elements.label: Spring workability of the fields
elements.description: Whether heavy machinery can work the fields early in spring without damaging the soil, set by soil structure and by how wet the soil is: soil work done when the soil is too wet can smear and compact it and form clods, by the Dutch cultivation guide, and in the climate scenarios more rain in spring leaves fewer moments to do it (Verstand et al., 2021, p. 25, on potatoes). It follows the soil's wetness within the season, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Ditch level (NAP)
elements.description: The water level Waterschap Scheldestromen holds in the island's ditches, relative to NAP, as its water level plans set it: Duiveland's plan sets a target level for each of its level areas, from 0.8 to 2.7 m below NAP, in most the summer level higher than the winter one, against nature's order, to prevent water damage in winter and drying in summer (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 37, 64–65). It moves from the winter level to the summer one in steps in March and April, as the weather and the farmers' soil work allow (p. 66). The level holds until the board carries out a new plan: Duiveland's study of 2021 drew up a new plan to replace the one in force since 1982 (pp. 5, 24), and the board checks each plan every three years and renews it at 17 years or once it no longer fits (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, pp. 16–17), so a Stock. On the island the board holds Schouwen's summer levels high on purpose to limit subsidence by peat compaction (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 45), and changes a level in soil prone to settling by no more than the land has subsided since (p. 50).
elements.simplification: One level for the year stands for the winter and summer levels a plan sets, in most of Duiveland's level areas the summer level the higher (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 64–65): spring workability and winter rain drained away follow the winter level through Polder drainage depth, held until the steps of March and April (p. 66), and seepage the level of either season. A raise of either level moves each link out the same way or leaves it unmoved, so B3, B4, R2, B11, B12 and R8 keep their polarity and mechanism. What it leaves out: a plan that raises only the summer level would, by inference, ease seepage without costing spring workability, which one level cannot show. The level is also taken as held, while in many areas where the summer level is set well above a low winter level it can usually be held only a few weeks before it sinks slowly into the soil, and without water supply, which the island lacks (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8), it may not be maintainable in a rainfall deficit (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, pp. 37, 66), so in a dry summer the level lies lower than set and, by inference, seepage is higher. That push comes from the weather, outside every named loop, so the same six loops keep their polarity and mechanism.

elements.label: Polder drainage depth
elements.description: How far below the surface the ditch levels lie in the island's polders (the drooglegging): the surface's elevation minus the ditch level, the difference on which the board defines its optimum (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 40). On a creek ridge studied for water storage the depth is over 1.5 m in winter in large parts (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 42). It follows the ditch level and the surface within the year, so an Auxiliary: where the land subsides under a level held, the depth shrinks until a new plan lowers the level, as the board's policy describes for peat (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, p. 13).

elements.label: Water board's plans to raise ditch levels
elements.description: The water level plans in which Waterschap Scheldestromen raises a polder's ditch levels, from the draft until their levels take effect. The board matches its levels to the land's use and soil, its principle that the level follows the land use: arable land 60 to 120 cm below the surface by soil, permanent grassland as a rule 20 cm less (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 29; 2025, pp. 5, 7, 19), weighing flooding, drought, fresh water and groundwater (2021c, p. 19), subsidence (2025, pp. 13–14) and a change's costs against its benefits (2025, p. 12). On Duiveland the plan of 2021 proposed studying a raise in 14 level areas, where levels had been kept low to store extreme rain, to enlarge the fresh water in the soil and give crops more moisture (2021a, p. 69). The general board adopts each plan (2025, p. 18); of its 30 members, 26 represent the residents and two the owners of unbuilt land, farmland included, appointed by ZLTO's board (Reglement voor het Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2025, arts. 6–7). A plan waits years for the works its levels need (Water board's plans to raise ditch levels → Polder drainage depth), so a Stock.
elements.simplification: The two seats on the general board for the owners of unbuilt land, farmland included, were a Constant driving these plans, and are in the description instead: no loop runs through a Constant, so no loop changes. What it leaves out: the seats cannot be set as an input of their own.

elements.label: Water board's pumping costs
elements.description: What Waterschap Scheldestromen spends on electricity for the pumping stations that hold the polders' ditch levels, by pumping out the water that reaches the ditches. Every polder on the island is pumped: on Schouwen all water flows to two pumping stations, which pump it over the dike into the Oosterschelde and the Grevelingen (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 24); low-lying Duiveland has a pumping station for each of its five drainage areas (2021a, p. 21). Across the board's area the cost follows the water pumped: in the dry year 2025 its water systems spent €1.1 million less on electricity than budgeted, for the drought (2026e, p. 18), and for 2026 it budgets about €4.8 million for the electricity of its sewage and polder pumping stations together, which extreme rain can raise by up to 25% (p. 55). No source read gives the island's share. A year's spending: an Auxiliary.
elements.simplification: Draws only the water coming in: Saline seepage and Winter rain drained away, which Ditch level (NAP) and Polder drainage depth already drive with the same sign, so every loop keeps its polarity; the rain the drains carry off the creek ridges and dunes, which Winter rain drained away leaves out, reaches the same pumping stations and rises with the same drainage depth, so drawing it would change no sign. What it leaves out: how high the water is lifted, on which no source read shows the costs depending.

ask actors.for: What its pumping stations on the island use in electricity a year, how much of the water they pump is seepage and how much rain, and how far the cost depends on how high they lift it: on Duiveland it measures the discharge at each pumping station (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021a, p. 24).

elements.label: Water board levy on farmland
elements.description: What Waterschap Scheldestromen charges on farmland for its water management, pumping included. The law charges those who hold unbuilt land by ownership, possession or a limited right (Waterschapswet, 2026, art. 117), which leaves out its tenants, at one rate per hectare (art. 121): €115.53 for 2026 (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026d, art. 6).

elements.label: Harvest lost to salt
elements.description: The conventional crops' harvest that salt in the root zone takes, over the island's fields still under them, in a season. On the island, farms where seepage pressure is high and the surface water is salty all year have stopped growing sensitive crops such as sown onions (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 31). Zeeland is among the coastal provinces where potatoes and barley lose considerable yield to salt (Deolu-Ajayi et al., 2024, p. 12). Salt's effect on yield builds up over weeks to months and is read over the season (Allen et al., 1998, ch. 8): within the year, so an Auxiliary.

elements.label: Margin given up on high-margin crops
elements.description: On the hectares a farm moves from its high-margin current crops, potatoes and sown onions, to new crops or to salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops: what the current crop would earn without salt less what the new crop or variety earns, a margin being revenue minus the crop's variable costs (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 1). What salt takes is Harvest lost to salt, so it is not counted here. Potatoes, beets, onions and field vegetables are the high-margin crops; the margin of protein crops is comparable to that of cereals and cannot compete with most other crops (Polman et al., 2026, p. 9); quinoa, in a study for Flanders, yields about 3 tonnes a hectare, sold at €1,100 a tonne under contract on a market still very small, against cultivation costs under contract of about €1,470 a hectare, storage and marketing left out (Cloet et al., 2024, p. 2). In the Netherlands, interviews on quinoa and seed potatoes on saline soil found the lack of economic benefits the main constraint on scaling them (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 276), and on Terschelling food grown on salt-affected soil costs more to produce than food grown with fresh water, the project relying on volunteers and, at its start, on subsidies (ten Dam et al., 2023, pp. 10, 13, 16). A season's crop: within the year.

elements.label: Farms with a successor
elements.description: Arable farms on the island whose farmer has someone to take the farm over. Nationally, in 2023, 43% of the 33,000 farms whose head is over 50 had a successor, against 40% in 2020, and 39% of the arable farms, the agricultural census asking three times in ten years (Agrimatie, 2024); no source read gives the island's figure.

ask actors.for: How many arable farmers on the island over 50 have a successor.

elements.label: Net price for new crops after transport
elements.description: What farmers on the island get for new crops once transport to the processor is paid, set by processors on and off the island. No source read gives what quinoa fetches: its cost price at the farm gate is 0.70 to 1.25 euro a kilo (van Loo, 2023, p. 79), most Dutch growers selling it under contract to one buyer (DutchNews.nl, 2026). The food market for halophytes is small and easily saturated (van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6), a Zeeland trader noting surpluses (FreshPlaza, 2018); no source read gives their price.
elements.simplification: Counts one net price for every new crop, though the description shows them sold differently: most Dutch quinoa growers selling under contract to one buyer, halophytes on a small food market that saturates easily. It assumes each crop's price rises alike with a plant nearby or more processing elsewhere. Per crop R7 runs through the same positive links, so it keeps its polarity and its mechanism; what the total leaves out is a price that rises for one crop and not another, which the semi-quantitative analysis cannot vary apart.

elements.label: Growers of new crops elsewhere
elements.description: Farmers off the island growing the same new crops, whose harvest a local plant could also process. More than two dozen farmers in the Netherlands grow quinoa, one of them at Vierhuizen in Groningen: most under contract with GreenFood50, its growers working about 200 hectares for 600 tonnes a year, and a few independently (DutchNews.nl, 2026); GreenFood50, founded in 2014, has had quinoa grown in the Netherlands since 2019 and in Belgium since 2021 (GreenFood50, n.d.).
elements.simplification: Holds the growers off the island fixed, though a plant on or near the island could draw growers near it off the island as it draws the island's own: GreenFood50 has its quinoa grown close to its processing facilities, to cut transport (GreenFood50, n.d.), and no source read shows whether a plant here would. The loop this leaves out, a local plant raising what nearby growers off the island get and so the harvest within its reach, has no minus sign and runs by R7's mechanism, so R7 and C7 keep their polarity and their story; leaving it out means that, in the CLD, a local plant reaches its volume from the island's own hectares alone.

elements.label: Processing of new crops elsewhere
elements.description: Plants outside Zeeland that buy and process new crops: where the island's growers can sell a new crop now, beside a local plant. For Dutch quinoa the sources read show one main buyer, GreenFood50 at Wageningen, which runs the chain from grower to customer and has its quinoa grown close to its processing facilities, which it does not locate (GreenFood50, n.d.), most Dutch growers under contract with it (DutchNews.nl, 2026).
elements.simplification: Counts the plants outside Zeeland that buy any new crop as one, while the sources in the description show a buyer outside Zeeland for quinoa alone; for the sea vegetables, Local processing capacity for new crops shows a grower and trader in Zeeland who sorts, packs and sells them. A Constant has no link in and lies on no loop, so no loop depends on the sum; what it leaves out is for which new crops a buyer outside Zeeland exists at all.

elements.label: Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties
elements.description: Hectares under salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops (potato, onion), which use the same machines, storage and know-how. Farmers grow one where they find it worthwhile against the variety they grow now. Such potato varieties exist and are tested in the Netherlands: of 13 cultivars from Dutch breeders and suppliers grown in the field on Texel from 2012 to 2018, Elgar and Rivola kept 90% of their yield up to a soil salinity above 7.5 dS/m, against 4 to 4.5 dS/m for five others (van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 2, 10); for onion, no source read shows one variety more tolerant than another. No source read shows them grown on the island or in Zeeland: stakeholders in the Dutch potato industry named salt-tolerant varieties as developed in the Netherlands mostly for arid countries, with no mention of domestic use (Aldrich et al., 2023, p. 38). Switching to salt- or drought-resistant varieties is among the drought adaptation measures van Duinen et al. (2015a, p. 1085) list for farmers in the south-west Netherlands, from a survey of 2013. A Stock: a field keeps the variety sown in it for the season, so the hectares hold until farmers sow again.

elements.label: Yield of salt-tolerant varieties on offer
elements.description: The yield of the salt-tolerant varieties of the current crops that breeders bring to market, where salt does not limit the crop, against the high-yielding varieties grown now; breeding lies outside the CLD's scale. Dutch breeders and suppliers sell potato cultivars that differ in salt tolerance: of 13 bought from them and tested in the field on Texel, Rivola, Elgar and '927' were more tolerant than the others on sandy soil (van Straten et al., 2021, pp. 2, 11). With no official label for salt tolerance, trading houses claim it for no variety, one of them saying only which suit saline soils best and worst, and salt tolerance is not yet among the ten traits that the salespeople of one trading house, endorsed by another, rank most important for a new variety (de Wit et al., 2022, pp. 271–272); stakeholders interviewed in the Dutch potato industry say the salt-tolerant seed potatoes bred in the Netherlands are mostly for export to arid countries such as Egypt and Morocco (Aldrich et al., 2023, pp. 38, 40). Tolerant varieties yield relatively little against common high-yielding ones without salt or under mild salt, and conventional breeding typically takes 10 to 15 years (van den Burg et al., 2024, pp. 3, 6). Measured in interviews across the Dutch potato chain and in field trials on Texel; none on the island.
elements.simplification: Holds the salt tolerance of the varieties on offer at that of the cultivars the description names, so only their yield varies. A variable holding both would have no one sign into Margin given up on high-margin crops, since tolerance and yield trade off (Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties → Margin given up on high-margin crops): a more tolerant variety that yields less raises what a hectare gives up, one that yields more lowers it. The yield is where the description shows tolerant varieties falling short of the high-yielding ones. What it leaves out: a more tolerant variety on offer losing less on each hectare at the same salinity, a strength of Adoption of salt-tolerant varieties → Harvest lost to salt, no variable. The element has no links in and is on no loop, so no loop changes.

elements.label: Machines and storage for the current crops
elements.description: The machines a farm owns that suit only one or a few crops (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45) and the buildings, machines and paving for storing its potatoes and onions (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 15, 17), a store for long keeping being a mostly insulated building with a cooling installation (Janssens et al., 2020, p. 5). Nationally an estimated 1,500 farms at least, mainly arable ones, had a store for long keeping with potatoes still in it on 1 April 2020, which takes a cooled store; taken as all arable, that is 40% of the 3,725 specialised arable farms growing ware potatoes (p. 7). Machines are depreciated at 8.2% a year, installations at 10% and buildings at 3% (p. 13, from KWIN 2018): about 12, 10 and 33 years, if that is a constant share of the purchase price. Machines, implements and installations are the main category of Dutch arable farms' investment (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19). No source read counts them on the island, where one farmer interviewed names mechanisation among the reasons for adding land (Dijkshoorn-Dekker et al., 2024, pp. 56–57).

elements.label: Capital lost on switching to new crops
elements.description: What the machines, storage and know-how of a farm's current crops would stop earning if it moved fields to a crop that cannot use them, less what it can sell them for. A store's costs do not fall when the crops in it take a smaller part of the rotation: they are sunk and cannot be earned back (Polman et al., 2026, pp. 15, 17), and other paths need new technology and skills while the old may not yet be written off (Bonnet & Tiktak, 2025, p. 45). It differs by what the farm moves to. Quinoa is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine harvester (van Loo, 2023, p. 75); adding protein crops leaves buildings and machines as they were (Polman et al., 2026, p. 4), and a store stands idle only once nothing it can hold is grown. A salt-tolerant variety of a current crop is planted, lifted and stored as that crop is, so it loses little of it, which no source read states. No source read says what a used harvester or store would fetch.
elements.simplification: Counts the capital a switch would write off as one value for every new crop, though the description shows it differing by what the farm moves to: quinoa is sown with standard equipment and harvested with a combine, while other paths need new technology and skills. For every new crop the loss is what that crop cannot use of the current crops' machines, storage and know-how, so it grows with what the farm owns for them and holds the farm to them: R3 keeps its polarity and its mechanism, and only its strength differs by destination, which the semi-quantitative analysis cannot vary apart, one adoption variable holding every new crop.

elements.label: Farmers' knowledge of new crops
elements.description: What the island's farmers know about growing and selling new crops, from their own fields, their neighbours' and advisers. For quinoa this knowledge is still thin in the Netherlands: research on growing it is relatively underdeveloped, and a grower harvested 2,000 kg from 4 hectares one year and 2,500 kg the next without knowing why, multiple interviewees agreeing that too little is known (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 269); what Dutch consumers want from it is under-researched (p. 270). Knowing that crops must cope with salt is a separate matter: most of Zeeland's farmers know it, yet still grow common salt-sensitive crops such as potato and wheat (Stuyt et al., 2016, as cited in van den Burg et al., 2024, p. 6). Measured in 32 interviews, 29 of them in the Netherlands and seven with farmers (de Wit et al., 2022, p. 266), and across Zeeland; none on the island.
elements.simplification: Counts what the island's farmers know of every new crop as one stock, as Adoption of new crops counts their hectares as one area, while the evidence in the description on knowing how to grow and sell them is for quinoa alone: it assumes that growing one new crop lowers the risk a farmer sees in all of them, which no source read shows. Per crop the loop through it stays reinforcing with the same mechanism, growing a crop teaching how to grow it and so lowering the risk seen in moving the next field to it; by inference the total makes that loop look stronger where farms spread their fields over new crops that teach little about each other.

elements.label: Spending on keeping the current crops
elements.description: What farms invest a year in carrying on with their current crops: wells and irrigation, drains, new machines and stores. On Dutch arable farms the main category of investment is machines, implements and installations (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 19, from national farm accounts); in Zeeland the water board's general rule lets a farm pump fresh groundwater for irrigation of more than 10 m³ an hour, up to 60 m³ an hour, 3,000 m³ a quarter and 8,000 m³ a year, without a permit but notified at least four weeks ahead, through a horizontal well, from a fresh body its map shows outside its vulnerable areas, one at least 15 m thick or reaching the geohydrological base (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1, 2.9 lid 2 h and 4.8 b and f), and in a creek-ridge cluster's estimate of 2022 a horizontal well for brackish water costs €25,000 to €40,000 (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 48–49); and most of the farmers in five quickscans on the island's eastern creek ridges have drains in part of their fields (p. 38). An Auxiliary: a year's spending, what it buys accumulating in Machines and storage for the current crops, the wells and drains in the delay on its link to Groundwater extraction for irrigation.

elements.label: Banks' risk assessment of farm loans
elements.description: The risk a bank sees in lending to an arable farm: more and more whether its operations will earn enough over the longer term to meet all its financial obligations, the expected income the limiting factor, beside its solvency and its land and buildings as security (van der Meulen et al., 2020, pp. 19, 47; Farjon et al., 2013, section Financiering van bedrijfsuitbreiding). Because arable returns swing from year to year, banks count farm loans as riskier despite the land as security, and the Basel capital rules steer them further toward lending on profitability and liquidity rather than on the value of the collateral (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47); financing a new concept whose returns are not yet proven they often count as a risk (p. 6). Rabobank's provisions for expected credit losses carried an adjustment of 87 million euro for climate risk at the end of 2024, set by sector on five events, drought and water scarcity among them (Rabobank, 2025, pp. 246–247). A public plan that may change what a farm can earn enters it before the plan is decided (Water board's plans to raise ditch levels → Banks' risk assessment of farm loans). A Stock: a bank's view of a farm holds until the bank revises it, and it weighs what the farm can earn over the longer term rather than in one year (Farm income → Banks' risk assessment of farm loans).

elements.label: Bank credit to farms
elements.description: New loans and refinancing that banks grant the island's arable farms in a year. Banks supply 90% of Dutch farms' long-term loans (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 20), whose total rose from 18 to 33 billion euro between 2001 and 2018, falling slightly in its last years (p. 19), and they have raised the repayments on land loans, ABN AMRO cutting the longest term for new farmland financing from fifty to forty years, a repayment of at least 2.5% a year (p. 47). No source read gives the banks' lending on the island.

elements.label: Debt payments
elements.description: The interest, commission and repayments farms owe their banks in a year. Interest and commission cost Dutch farms about 22,000 euro each in 2018, down from 30,000 in 2014 as interest rates fell (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 20); on arable farms interest was 8% of the costs they paid in 2018, against 12% in 2001, 2006 and 2011 (p. 57). The repayment follows mainly from the loan's size, term and schedule (ABN AMRO, n.d.-a), and banks have raised the repayments on land loans, ABN AMRO to at least 2.5% a year on new land loans (van der Meulen et al., 2020, p. 47). No source read gives the island's farms' payments.

elements.label: World prices of conventional crops
elements.description: The prices of potatoes, onions and sugar beet on the markets the island's crops are sold on, which its farms cannot move: what carrying on is weighed against. They form in an international market by supply and demand (Minister van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, 2018), moved by the harvests of north-west Europe and beyond, whose good harvests lowered arable prices in 2025 (van der Meulen, 2025; for potatoes, Janssens et al., 2020, p. 8). The Netherlands was the world's largest onion exporter in 2016, and by a rough estimate about 80% of Dutch onions are processed in Zeeland (Minister van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, 2018); onions are rarely sold under fixed-price contracts agreed in advance, so their price can swing (Bogosavac, 2018). The potato processors export an estimated 80% of their frozen products, and buy 90 to 95% of their potatoes under contract or in a pool, the rest free (Janssens et al., 2020, pp. 1, 7), a contract's base price published each year for four processors (p. 11). No source read here gives how the beet price is set.

elements.label: Farmers' trust in government
elements.description: How far the island's farmers expect the public bodies that plan for its water and land to keep their commitments (compensation, their say over their land). Trust is typically created slowly and can be destroyed in an instant, and once lost may take a long time to rebuild (Slovic, 1993, p. 677, as a long-known quality of trust; Remkes, 2022, p. 19). No source read measures it on the island: in 2013, 141 farmers in the south-west Netherlands, 16 of the survey's 142 on Schouwen-Duiveland, averaged 2.64 on a seven-point scale of trust in their water board on drought (van Duinen et al., 2015b, pp. 745–749), and one submission to the Province in 2021, by an engineer (Ir.) arguing for a fresh Grevelingen lake, says the island's farmers no longer trust the Province, which it says still appears unwilling to act adequately on salinisation and is dragging its feet on fresh-water supply (Lases, 2021, p. 2). From outside the island's scale comes national policy changed or dropped: plans announced and then changed, postponed or stopped, which the National Ombudsman, from interviews with 32 farmers across the country, concludes has left the government unreliable for them (Nationale ombudsman, 2026, pp. 8, 15, 40), and a gap of trust with 'The Hague' (Remkes, 2022, p. 13). The same farmers feel that decisions about their farm, land or future are prepared elsewhere, that they can react only late or to a limited extent, and that policymakers ignore their input; the Ombudsman concludes that this leads to a lack of trust in government (Nationale ombudsman, 2026, pp. 24–25). Whether the island's farmers carry that over to the water board, the Province and the municipality, no source read shows: a question for the group model building session.

elements.label: Farmers' wish to keep their land
elements.description: How strongly farmers hold on to their land beyond its money value: family land, growing up on it. In the Krimpenerwaard, where a land-use plan designated farmland for nature with expropriation as its last step, owners who kept their land and turned it into nature themselves named the wish not to lose it, from an emotional bond with it, as an important reason, for one farm weighing more than moving (Kamphorst et al., 2025, pp. 11, 49, 68); selling land held for generations often weighs heavily, though one farmer's father had advised getting out if he could (p. 54). At succession the farm customarily passes to one child at its low agricultural value, the other children giving up part of their inheritance so that the parental farm can continue (Luijt, 2007, pp. 23, 25). In interviews with 20 owners in the Netherlands facing a government plan on their land, owners described a strong emotional involvement in the plans, touching their social life and well-being, against government professionals who could end their work at five o'clock (Holtslag-Broekhof et al., 2016, pp. 172, 177). Measured among 14 owners interviewed in the Krimpenerwaard, dairy farms and private owners on peat, among 20 across the Netherlands, and nationally for succession; no source read measures it on the island or among arable farmers. Whether anything on the map moves it, at succession perhaps, is a question for the group model building session.

elements.label: Freshwater lens thickness under creek ridges and dunes
elements.description: The thickness of the fresh groundwater under the island's sandy creek ridges and dunes, down to the middle of the mixing zone with the saline groundwater: 5 to 15 m under the creek ridges (de Louw et al., 2011, pp. 3667, 3673, 3675, measured on the island), reaching about 30 m under the creek ridges and the dunes and nearly 100 m under the dunes (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 10). The lens farmers pump: the water board's rules let them pump it for irrigation without a permit, up to 60 m³ an hour, 3,000 m³ a quarter and 8,000 m³ a year and notified at least four weeks ahead, where its map shows a fresh groundwater body outside its vulnerable areas, one at least 15 m thick or reaching the geohydrological base (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1 and 4.8 b and f), and some farmers take water from it through a deep drain, one, a livestock farm, irrigating from two (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 38, 40). A Stock: it grows and thins over years (Freshwater storage measures → this lens).

elements.label: Pumping the water board allows
elements.description: The volume the island's farms may pump a year under Waterschap Scheldestromen's rules. Where: without a permit but notified at least four weeks ahead, for irrigation of more than 10 m³ an hour, up to 60 m³ an hour, 3,000 m³ a quarter and 8,000 m³ a year, from a fresh groundwater body the board's map shows outside its vulnerable areas, one at least 15 m thick or reaching the geohydrological base (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026f, arts. 1.1 and 4.8 b and f). How: a horizontal well at most 6 m below the surface and 80 to 200 m long, at least 200 m from the next well and 50 m from a neighbour's field. How much: at most 800 m³ per hectare and 8,000 m³ per well a year, set by the balance between what rain recharges, the irrigation water and the extraction, so the fresh stock lasts and the fresh-salt boundary does not rise (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b, art. 2.9 and its explanation). Extractions rose in recent dry years, and the province and the water board talk of registering the volumes more precisely (Gedeputeerde Staten van Zeeland, 2021); no source read shows the farms' pumping changing the rules, the 2026 revision keeping the cap. A Stock: a notified well pumps until the board forbids it (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2026b).

elements.label: Knowledge of how storage works on the island
elements.description: What the island's farmers, their advisers and contractors know of how freshwater storage works on the island: how the soil and groundwater behave, and what a measure costs, risks and yields. The knowledge from the pilots has not yet been translated to the island's soil, water and farm conditions, which leaves much uncertainty about building a measure, its costs, its management, its risks and its gain (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 11), and local advisers and farmers understand too little of how the soil and groundwater system works (p. 12). It builds up as measures are built and monitored, so a Stock. Outside the island's farms, the project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water shapes it, its final report by authors from Deltares, KWR, Acacia Water and Buro Waterfront (Kaandorp et al., 2022, pp. 2–3): it drew up quickscan advice for 13 farmers (p. 9) and feasibility studies for clusters of farms (pp. 30, 33, 40), and made methods, maps and tools available with which farmers and advisers can go on by themselves (pp. 4, 55). The EU co-funded that project (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-a) and paid half of a later one, of Acacia Water, Deltares, Delphy, the trial farm Rusthoeve, three farms and the municipality, which demonstrated and monitored new drainage on the island for figures and guidelines on building, managing and maintaining it (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-b); the programme of its closing meeting had Acacia Water, Deltares and Delphy explain its yield and effect (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, 2024).

elements.label: Salt in the ditch water
elements.description: The salinity of the water in the island's ditches, the water a farm would irrigate with or infiltrate. All water on Schouwen runs through the water board's main ditches and capillaries to its two pumping stations, which pump the surplus over the dike into the Oosterschelde and the Grevelingenmeer (Waterschap Scheldestromen, 2021b, p. 24), and in most of Duiveland the ditches catch the salt or brackish seepage from below (2021a, p. 20). In the low polders of the island's west the surface water is brackish to salt (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 27); in one area studied, a cluster of creek ridges in the east of the island, the main ditches measured 5 to 15 mS/cm and the secondary ditches round the fields 1 to 5, with indications that the main ditches are less brackish after rain, as drained rain mixes in, and in dry periods their salt seeming partly to come from salt surface water brought in from elsewhere (pp. 38, 40, 42). The CLD draws salt taking fresh water away by amount, the lenses thinning, and here by quality. An Auxiliary: it follows the seepage and the rain within the season. No actor decides it: the water board reaches it through the ditch level and the seepage (Ditch level (NAP) → Saline seepage (kwel)), as it reaches the lens.

elements.label: Water demand of the crop mix
elements.description: The fresh water the island's crops need in the growing season, summed over the crop plan: what the rotation uses when it has enough water, its evapotranspiration, set by the weather and by each crop and its stage of growth (Allen et al., 1998, FAO-56, a guide to crop water use that holds wherever the crop grows). The crops that earn the most also have the greatest water need and often a limited root system (Delphy, 2023, p. 48), and for the island's farms Delphy puts the total water need at about 3.5 million m³ (p. 41). No link comes from the new crops: no source read shows one needing less water than the crop it replaces when both have enough, the need this variable sums. Quinoa copes with little water, still yielding grain on 270 mm (van Loo, 2023, p. 75), which acts in the farmers' choice (Crop water shortfall → Fields moved to new crops), not here; fibre crops and legumes may replace winter wheat, and flax needs water too (Delphy, 2023, p. 48). It follows the rotation, set each year: an Auxiliary. The farmers decide the crop mix, so it has no actor of its own.

elements.label: Trials and pilots on the island
elements.description: The trials, pilots and demonstrations that parties beside the farmers run on the island and for its farms, each showing what a measure or a crop does under the island's conditions. The Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland started officially in January 2019 as a place for parties who want to innovate together, to speed up the island's move to self-sufficient water management (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 8); its project Samenwerken voor Zoet Water (2020–2022), carried out with Deltares, KWR, Acacia Water, Agrarisch Schouwen-Duiveland and the municipality (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-a), made quickscans for 13 farmers (Kaandorp et al., 2022, p. 9), and a later one, of Acacia Water, Deltares, Delphy, the trial farm Rusthoeve, three farms and the municipality, demonstrated and monitored new drainage on the island (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, n.d.-b), laid at Kerkwerve and Dreischor (Living Lab Schouwen-Duiveland, 2023). For crops, Delphy, with ZLTO and Saeftinghe Zilt, researched saline cultivation in 2014–2018 (Delphy, 2023, p. 49), and the trial farm Rusthoeve, at Colijnsplaat on Noord-Beveland, has experimented with crops since 2014 and laid out irrigation trials after 2018 (pp. 9, 19, 20, 24). A Constant: no source read shows the farms' choices moving the trials, so whether the trials answer what farmers do or ask for is a question for the group model building session.

elements.label: Perceived risk of switching
elements.description: How much a farmer expects to lose by moving a field to a new crop, before moving it: a failed yield, no buyer, a low price, too little water, carried by the farm. It drives the decision before a switch, where Margin given up on high-margin crops is the outcome after it; Farmers' knowledge of new crops is whether a farmer knows how, this who pays when it fails. On the island, larger business risks slow innovation (Delphy, 2023, p. 6), crops grow so costly that they may not fail (p. 13), and the cost of innovative solutions lies mainly with the farmer while they are not yet proven, so investing carries a risk (p. 50). In a survey of farmers in the south-west Netherlands (2013), a higher perceived cost of drought measures lowered their adaptation and trust in their own competence raised it, both parts of how farmers appraise their ability to cope (van Duinen et al., 2015a, pp. 1089, 1091). Whether it runs through others' successes and failures is a question for the group model building session. An Auxiliary: it follows what farmers know and the contracts on offer. No actor: a perception, not a decision.

elements.label: Buyer contracts for new crops
elements.description: Hectares of new or alternative crops that buyers contract with the island's farmers before the season.
